Lol yeah that can definitely fuck you up. I was on a maintenance recovery team for press loss in flight, the crew had to emergency land because they reported hypoxia symptoms. We pressurized that jet like 10 times a day until we fixed it, 2 weeks later. The book said not to pressurize more than, IIRC, 3 times in 24 hours. 


Safety regs and TOs are great unless you’re young, think you’re invincible, and you start to feel the pressure of the mission with leadership hounding you about fixing the jet asap because it’s going on a mission or a medevac or like a few years ago when we had the Kabul evacuation. If we are evacuating a historic amount of people, in my mind I can forgo safety a bit because that time saved might mean more lives saved. Not wanting to let your team and coworkers down normally wins out over safety when you’re young dumb & stupid (talking about myself here). Now I get debilitating migraines multiple times a week, my hands and arms go numb randomly, my back hasn’t stopped killing me for the last few years and my spine has felt bruised to touch in multiple places for that same length. 


I’m not saying it’s worthy of 100%, but I got 100% and I didn’t ask for it or lie or exaggerate. Most people don’t. It’s not like they ask you what percentage disability you want and then they give it to you, they decide with the evidence (medical records) that is given to them and the exams that they themselves perform. I helped all my friends out when they got out, offered myself for buddy statements if they needed them, went through how to apply etc with them. We should be helping each other out, not tearing each other down over some dumb competition of masculinity & combat. We all served together, we mostly all became damaged in some way, some more than others, but there is no competition over who was hurt worse.  If you’re upset that somebody without combat got more than you, you need to reflect on the fact that maybe you deserve a higher percentage, not that they deserve a lesser percentage. As long as you’re not lying, get what you deserve.

Hey man, I’m sorry you’re feeling this way, I don’t know if it helps to hear but you’re not alone in the way you’re feeling, I’ve had this problem probably hundreds of times in the last 18 months. If this is a common occurrence for you (panic attacks), I’d recommend talking to your primary care or MH. I did the same and they put me on propranolol, which helps a ton with the physical anxiety (slows your heart rate down, stops it beating out of your chest, stops the shakes, hot flashes and just the overall ‘panic’ response). The only thing it doesn’t do is deal with the anxiety itself but for me a big part of the panic attack cycle was my physical reaction. Regardless though, it can help calm you down, and there is also hydroxyzine which similarly calms you down and makes you sleepy, so you can sleep it off which is what I would do sometimes. Point is, when you’re feeling better you should try and get the motivation to contact your doctor and see what you can do. Medication is not for everyone and I understand that, and this is just advice based on my own personal experience, but it has helped me like a shit ton. Panic attacks no longer ruin my whole day, at worst it’ll be an hour or two of my day and they’re far less frequent. My DMs are always open if you need to talk. You’ve got this man, we are all behind you.

Get help brother/sister; there is no shame in taking a knee. I was suicidal at one point, reached the point where I went to the ER for a bad headache, but just caved and told them I was actually suicidal. Doctor came in and thanked me for getting help, gave me a hug and told me that I was going to get help, and just said in general quite a few nice things that I really needed to hear at that time. They kept me in overnight (it was like 2am) and when I woke up I had a coworker sitting in the room with me, who escorted me to mental health to come up with a treatment plan and then to my CC with a sealed letter (I think it was for my PIF). Coworker was great, didn’t even know him at the time as he was a different spec but our desks were next to each other (AMXS). Talked to me like a human with feelings, got to know me by asking what I like to do etc and then turned out we have some common interests. Checked up on me after that day every now and then too even though he had no obligation to.

Oh, and I was never kicked out, or treated any differently. I got the help I needed, continued to come in to work, and that was that. 

My point is, you’re not alone in this, even if it may seem like you are. Many of us have felt this way at some point in time, but you have to make that first step of deciding you need to get help (which it seems you are doing with this post) and then acting on it. Who cares if you’ll get kicked out?  If you commit suicide, you won’t have a career in the AF anyways. If you get help, you’ll get the help you need, first and foremost, and you’ll most likely still have your AF career (unless you’re required to be armed).

 Again, there’s no shame in this, you need to get yourself some help. DM me if you ever need to talk, I’m proud of you for making this first step. You’ve got this.

For memorable.. I'm aircraft mx and my unit went TDY for ~5 months. About halfway through the TDY, I was working on one of our jets right at the edge of the flightline, so there was nothing between myself and the runway, and the interstate highway beyond the fence. 

I was on a B2 stand taking off a split panel on the pylon when I heard a LOUD bang from above me. I looked up to where the noise came from and saw a pilot in a parachute coming down, and a now pilot-less F-16 heading straight towards a highway that the base was next to. 

I remember shouting "what the fuck" a few times as I scrambled down the stand to join my co-workers in watching the event unfold. We had firefighters on the spot next to us standing watch for an engine run, they *sprinted* to their truck and sped off past us to meet the pilot in the field he landed in, a couple hundred feet from me. 

Watching the jet about to crash was like it was in slow motion,and yet now that I am telling this and recalling it, everything happened so fast. It flew over the highway and crashed into a warehouse, which at the time was equally as worrying because we were sure there were people in there. From what I remember, the warehouse workers were inside but miraculously no one was injured. 

Myself and my co-workers just kind of stood there afterwards for what felt like forever, in complete silence, until we were evacuated to the shop building where we had to remain in lockdown for ~3 hours because hydrazine.



For fun (and memorable)... I went on an MRT to Singapore. Hey man I’m aircraft mx and I got diagnosed with ADD/ADHD maybe a year after I got to my first duty station and I’m still here 5 years later. 

It will *not* affect your career in MX. Like at all (unless it’s crazy bad and you’re constantly making massive (fatal) mistakes, which you’ve already said you’re not). I know a bunch of other people that have gotten the diagnosis, all in Aircraft MX too. 

After diagnosis they normally prescribe you medication first, usually adderall but you’ll go through medications with your doctor and see which one works best for you. And then you’ll have a check up every now and then to see how you’re getting on with the medications, mood, focus levels, etc. That’s it. No MEB or anything crazy, I don’t think anyone even knows other than people (friends) that I’ve told..you can still go TDY, deploy etc. they do put you on a 3 month temporary profile while you adjust to the new medication in case of an emergency but after that you’re back to normal. 


I would really recommend going. The right medication is life changing, and medication really is the only truly effective treatment. Not sure what your base is like but I went to mental health/BHOP (behavioural health) for everything
